How to Check Tyre Pressure at Home

Checking your tyre pressure is one of the easiest car jobs you can do at home. It takes about five minutes and you only need a gauge. In this guide we explain how to check tyre pressure, what the numbers mean and how often you should do it.

Table of Contents

  • Why Tyre Pressure Matters
  • What You Need
  • Step by Step

Why Tyre Pressure Matters

Tyre pressure matters a lot more than most drivers think. When your tyres have the right amount of air, the car brakes better, steers better and uses less fuel. When the pressure is too low, the tyre flexes more, gets hot and wears out on the edges. When the pressure is too high, the middle of the tread wears faster and the car can feel bouncy and less stable on wet roads.

Under-inflated tyres are also a safety problem. A tyre that is very low on air can overheat on a long motorway drive, and in the worst case it can fail. The NHTSA tyre safety page explains why checking pressure every month is a good habit for every driver.

What You Need

You do not need special tools to check your tyres. Most people already have everything at home or can buy it cheaply at a petrol station or car shop.

  • A tyre pressure gauge (digital or dial type)
  • An air compressor or access to a petrol station air pump
  • The recommended pressure for your car, which is on the door sticker or in the handbook

Step by Step

The best time to check tyre pressure is in the morning, before you drive. Driving warms the tyres up and warm air gives a higher reading, so a cold check is more accurate. If you have already driven, wait at least three hours before you check.

  1. Find the recommended pressure on the sticker inside the driver door or in your handbook.
  2. Take the cap off the valve on the first tyre and keep it somewhere safe.
  3. Press the gauge firmly onto the valve until the hissing stops and read the number.
  4. Add air if the reading is too low, or press the small pin in the valve to let air out if it is too high.
  5. Check again, put the cap back on and repeat for the other tyres and the spare.

Many people forget the spare wheel. It is a good idea to check it at the same time, because a flat spare is no help when you get a puncture on the side of the road.

Where to Find the Right Pressure

The right pressure for your car is set by the car maker, not by the tyre maker. You can find it on a sticker in the driver door frame, inside the fuel filler flap or in the owner's handbook. The number on the tyre sidewall is the maximum pressure the tyre can hold, and it is not the pressure you should use every day. You can learn more in our guide on how to read tyre sidewall markings.

Some cars list two sets of numbers: one for normal driving and one for a full load. If you are carrying heavy luggage, a roof box or a full car of passengers, use the higher numbers for that trip and go back to the normal numbers afterwards.

How Often Should You Check?

Most experts say you should check your tyre pressure at least once a month and before every long trip. Tyres lose a little air over time even when there is nothing wrong with them. Changes in temperature also change the pressure, so it is worth checking more often when the weather turns cold in autumn.

If one tyre keeps losing air faster than the others, it may have a slow puncture or a leaking valve. In that case a tyre shop should look at it, because a slow leak can turn into a flat tyre at the worst possible moment.

Common Mistakes

The most common mistake is checking the tyres after a long drive, when they are hot. Another mistake is using the number printed on the tyre instead of the number from the car maker. Some drivers also trust the look of the tyre, but a tyre can be quite low on air and still look normal, especially with modern low-profile tyres.

Finally, cheap pencil gauges can be a few units out. If your readings seem strange, compare your gauge with the one at a petrol station or buy a better digital gauge. A good gauge does not cost much and it will last for years.
